nodes.question: What term does Archer use to describe the new forms of sustainability reporting in the text?
nodes.answer: Archer refers to this new form of sustainability reporting as "data driven sustainability."
nodes.paragraph: ( 2022 ), writing almost a decade later, observe that Australia-Oceania is the only region in the world where farm-based food security studies are rare compared to water security studies a gap this research addresses. Data-driven climate solutions There is a growing body of work on climate solutions and how these intersect with primary production. Central to solutions is measurement, significantly enhanced through advances in digital technology that have resulted in the proliferation of data. The Australian pastoral industry has become one of the most recent industries to be subject to what Archer ( 2021 :284) terms data driven sustainability . He describes a socio-technical imaginary of neoliberal sustainability (Archer 2021 :282) whereby sustainability reporting is now dependent upon data from intense and invasive regimes of monitoring and surveillance. Gale et al., (2017:77) refer to this as ICT-induced disintermediation , as remote surveillance enables new flows and arrangements of information, by-passing key stakeholders such as pro - ducers and enabling timely verification without the need for onsite audits. Whilst earlier forms of sustainability gover - nance relied on analogue data, Archer ( 2021 ) cautions that digitised forms of surveillance differ in that they are auto - mated.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Industry, innovation and infrastructure|Public-private synergy|Sustainability standards_qna_001
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What are the two critical theoretical/philosophical traditions on which the critical sustainability science research program is founded?
nodes.answer: The two critical theoretical/philosophical traditions are critical realism and historical materialism.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract The objective of this paper is to present a critical sustainability science research program, which is founded on two critical theoretical/philosophical traditions: critical realism and historical materialism. We elaborate these traditions to clarify what they can analytically offer to socioecological analyses in sustainability science and emphasize their prospective contributions to sustainability transitions and transformations. A critical sustainability science research program can facilitate bridging the natural and social sciences, provide crucial insights into social conditions and processes that drive ongoing and concerning environmental changes, identify often underexplored socioecological conditions for sustainability transitions/transforma- tions, and reveal structural process that can advance or impede them. The critical sustainability science approach offers an alternative to both mainstream and (critical) idealist/culturalist approaches in sustainability research. Keywords Socioecological theory Methodology Transitions Transformations Critical realism Historical materialism Introduction Much scientific research engages with matters of environ- ment and sustainability. Here, the focus will be on the field of sustainability science. This area of research can be defined as one that brings together different strands of scholarship on environmental issues from the natural sciences, social sci- ences, and humanities (Spangenberg 2011).

nodes.question: Which two critical theoretical/philosophical traditions are proposed for incorporation into sustainability science?
nodes.answer: The two traditions proposed for incorporation are critical realism and historical materialism.

But there is also a tendency in the field to neglect decades and even centuries of theoretical traditions and method- ological efforts to analyze and apprehend the world we inhabit (Longo et al. 2021a, b). While it can be tempting to dismiss long-standing traditions because of their appar - ent failure to do something about problems that persist, like climate change (e.g., O Brien 2016), we start from a rather modest, sociologically informed position regard- ing the relationship between science and societal change. We propose that some existing approaches, such as those which we will elaborate here, have crucial dimensions that often get neglected, misunderstood, or superficially applied, which has limited their potential contributions to sustainability science. Rectifying this does not guarantee that sufficient action will follow but the possibilities to produce well-targeted actions are enhanced. The objective of this paper is to clarify the analytical contributions, and we argue the necessity, of incorporat - ing specific critical theoretical/philosophical traditions into sustainability science: namely, critical realism and historical materialism. While scholars within the field may be familiar with (and have employed) the elements of either or both, they have not yet been brought together and articulated into a distinct sustainability science approach.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Industry, innovation and infrastructure|Public-private synergy|Sustainability standards_qna_003
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: How does critical sustainability science differ from other culturally based critical approaches?
nodes.answer: Critical sustainability science is built on a realist/materialist and dialectical foundation, contrasting with other approaches like post-structuralist, post-modernist, humanist, and Marxist critical theories.
nodes.paragraph: It is an analysis based in the deep-seated interrogation that lies at the heart of scientific inquiry and the manner to address sustainability problems, irrespective of the ideological con - frontations or the powerful actors it challenges, whether they be in the political, economic, or scientific realms. A grounding aspect of this approach is its scrutinty of taken-for-granted social conditions and assumptions. A criti- cal analysis is one that judiciously examines the prevailing social order and takes seriously the possibility and even the necessity for alternatives (Marcuse 2013). As such, it is indispensable for what contemporary sustainability science often refers to as sustainability transitions or transformations (e.g., Alonso-Adame et al. 2024; Davelaar 2021; Sahle et al. 2024a, b). Critical sustainability science draws fundamentally on the logic of science, even though it can and often does interrogate the institution of science (York 2021; York and Clark 2010). Importantly, in opposition to other cul- turally based critical approaches including for example post-structuralist, -modernist, -humanist, -Marxist criti- cal sustainability science is erected on a realist/materialist and dialectical footing.

nodes.question: What philosophy of science do the authors argue is necessary for tackling grand challenges in sustainability?
nodes.answer: The authors argue that an explicit philosophy of science based on critical realism is necessary for tackling grand challenges in sustainability.
nodes.paragraph: This foundation offers a unique approach for critical sustainability science. A sustainability science that takes (critical) realism seriously Sustainability science has been defined as a field of research interested in understanding the interactions between natural and social systems with the aim of facilitating sustainabil- ity transformations (Kates 2011). Other traits ascribed to the field relate to how it is problem and solution oriented as opposed to simply curiosity-driven (Doran et al. 2017 ; Spangenberg 2011), as evidenced by its namesake journal foregrounding the promotion of science-based predic- tions in its description of scope (Springer Nature 2023). Yet, the value proposition for theory in sustainability sci- ence remains questionable at best (Schl ter et al. 2022). It is our contention that sustainability transitions and transfor - mations, especially those capable of tackling today S grand challenges (e.g., climate change, food security, biodiversity loss), require explicit support from an explicit philosophy of science and related social theory. We arrive at this position through a commitment to the principles of realism critical realism, to be precise (Bhaskar 2013).

nodes.question: What role do well-designed sustainability metrics play in agricultural practices?
nodes.answer: They ensure transparency and rigor within the measurement process.
nodes.paragraph: 2021). Monitoring and measurement of agricultural practices can support progress towards long-term sustainability and support sustainable development (Calleros-Islas 2019), while the implementation of well-designed sustainability metrics can ensure transparency and rigor within the meas- urement process (Fanzo et al. 2021). Further, this can guide accountability of key agricultural systems stakeholders and the implementation of evidence-based policy for supporting more sustainable production (B hringer and Jochem 2007; Fanzo et al. 2021). For clarity, this review discusses methods for evaluating on-farm sustainability, which may incorporate indicators, metrics, tools or frameworks used to measure sustainability performance of an agricultural operation; this measurement generally occurs across one or more sustain- ability pillars (FAO 2014). A pillar represents a domain or category of sustainability that is relevant to agriculture; each pillar consists of qualitative or quantitative indicators that are utilised to monitor or benchmark the progress in rela- tion to a sustainability target. This review will utilise the terminology Comprehensive Assessment Instrument (CAI), or instrument when referring to agricultural sustainability assessment methods. nodes.question: What framework is presented in the paragraph for applying concepts of sustainability?
nodes.answer: The paragraph presents a practical kinship circle framework for broader educational applications in sustainability and environmental ethics.
nodes.paragraph: Beginning with the individual level, we encourage relearning what it means to be human, our place in the con- stellation of life, and the human responsibility to reaffirm our relations to Earth S Land. For the community, we recognize the vast collection of lived experiences, to rebuild our ability to think, listen, and be in kinship with the world as a relative. From the global scale, we focus on migration, particularly invasive species, to shift reigning perspectives on move- ment that elucidate the Earth as being alive and comprised of living beings. For each scale, we posit that by practicing relationships with responsibility, reciprocity, and respect toward all kin (relations based on interrelatedness of kinds) and kith (relations based on knowledge of place), humans may embody an ethic of sustainability that the Earth, and all Her inhabitants, require. Finally, we present a practical kinship circle framework for applying these concepts for broader educational applications in sustainability and envi- ronmental ethics. 1.2 Positionality As a kinship group, we use place-based knowledge and practices to understand how to build relationships with land, water, and other-than-humans.

nodes.question: What are the two types of sustainability discussed by scholars in the paragraph?
nodes.answer: The two types of sustainability discussed are weak sustainability and strong sustainability.
nodes.paragraph: 2024 ; Wudu et al. 2023 ). Sustainable practices aim to reduce our ecological foot - print and safeguard natural resources(Chakraborty and Thakur 2019 ; Galli et al. 2015 ; Gonzalez-Redin et al. 2024 ; Wiedmann and Barrett 2010 ). Meanwhile, the economic aspect of sustainability remains a topic of debate(Wilson 2023 ). Scholars discuss weak and strong sustainability, recognizing the importance of economic growth while seeking ways to decouple it from environ - mental harm(Hediger 2006 ; Islar et al. 2024 ; Neumayer 2013 ). This involves using fewer resources per unit of output while still promoting overall development. Lastly, social sustainability ensures that people do not encounter structural barriers(Ki jer and Langergaard 2023 ; Miller 2023 ). It encompasses health, influence, competence, impartiality, and meaning-making(Wolff and Ehrstr m 2020 ). Emphasizing equity, social justice, and community well-being, social sustainability contrib - utes to a holistic vision of a sustainable world(Amster 2020 ; Husgafvel 2021 ; Partridge 2014 ; ilenskyt et al. 2024 ).

nodes.question: Why are Sri Lanka and the U.S. easily comparable for economic, environmental, and social sustainability in apparel production for workers?
nodes.answer: Sri Lanka and the U.S. both have excellent publicly available statistics on worker wages and health and safety information, making it easy to compare their sustainability in apparel production.

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: How do the values of economic sustainability indicators differ between U.S. and Sri Lankan based production?
nodes.answer: In U.S. based production, 100% of labour hours are paid below 4 * poverty line, while in Sri Lankan based production, only 20% of labour hours are paid below 4 * poverty line.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Industry, innovation and infrastructure|Public-private synergy|Sustainability standards_qna_012
nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: What is the significance of ISO 14,040:2006 in the context of sustainability practices in businesses?
nodes.answer: ISO 14,040:2006 is a standard set by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) that outlines guidelines for conducting life cycle assessments. This standard helps businesses evaluate the environmental impacts of their products and processes, enabling them to make more sustainable decisions.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Industry, innovation and infrastructure|Public-private synergy|Sustainability standards_qna_013
nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: What is sustainability disclosure, and how is it defined in the context of corporate information?
nodes.answer: Sustainability disclosure refers to a public, voluntary, non-financial disclosure of corporate information, including economic, social, and environmental impacts of businesses. It is a way for companies to communicate their commitment to sustainability and transparency.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Industry, innovation and infrastructure|Public-private synergy|Sustainability standards_qna_014
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: Why is sustainability reporting considered an elaborate and technically complex process despite the existence of reporting standards like GRI and AA1000?
nodes.answer: Sustainability reporting remains complex due to the wide range of non-financial information companies need to disclose, such as Sustainable Development Goals and business policies, which can vary in format and content based on individual company preferences.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Industry, innovation and infrastructure|Public-private synergy|Sustainability standards_qna_015
nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: Why are sustainability reports in the fashion industry not externally validated like financial reports?
nodes.answer: Sustainability reports lack external validation because there are no disclosure mandates or mechanisms for disclosure auditing, unlike financial reporting which has established standards and regulatory oversight.

nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: What international standards and guidelines form the basis for the method used to measure environmental impacts in the food chain?
nodes.answer: The method is based on international LCA standards like ISO 14,040 and ISO 14,044 LEAP guidelines, and Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) set by the European Commission.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Industry, innovation and infrastructure|Public-private synergy|Sustainability standards_qna_017
nodes.label: Strategy
nodes.question: What is the purpose of the themes and sub-themes within the SAFA guidelines?
nodes.answer: The themes and sub-themes within the SAFA guidelines are used for formulating sustainability objectives and indicators to measure sustainability criteria.
nodes.paragraph: 2017). The SAFA guidelines (FAO 2014) provide a framework for assessing the benefits and trade-offs of agriculture and food system practices on different sustainability issues. The guidelines are organised under the broader categories of environment, social, economy and governance, which are used for structuring the results of the review. These are further distinguished into themes and sub-themes with for - mulated sustainability objectives and indicators to measure sustainability criteria. Over the last years, the guidelines have been used to study the impact of livestock systems in various contexts (Cammarata et al. 2021; P rez-Lombardini et al. 2021; Niloofar et al. 2023). The range and structure of indicators within SAFA provides an overarching reference point for structuring the analysis. Complementing the One Health concept, which under - lines the strong connection between animal and human health, the One Welfare approach relates the wellbeing of animals to that of humans and recognizes their intercon- nections with the environment (Pinillos et al. 2016). Con- sidering these interactions makes it possible to detect and capitalize on direct and indirect benefits of one dimension on the other and thereby enables a holistic way to increase both human and animal welfare on a global scale (ibid.).
